name: ʿAlwa
roles: mother of Muḥammad IV, Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl, Fāṭima bint Ismāʿīl, Maryam bint Ismāʿīl

name: Ibn al-Khaṭīb
note: In the game the ablest man at court (88/79/84). Given command of the host against Aragon in May 1339 (Trent's account). By 8 July 1341 he had left Granada: the save of 8 September 1341 has him in Castile as Frederick ibn al-Khaṭīb, Catholic and Castilian, an admiral from 8 July 1341. On 6 January 1366 he led Castile's last field army, 950 men, at San Clemente, and Murād destroyed it. He himself survived (save of 5 April 1366).

name: Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl
note: Elder brother of Yūsuf I. Regent of Granada from 9 August 1351 until the sultan's return on 7 April 1352, while he made the Hajj (the chronicle's choice; the game named a Naṣr al-Stijjai). Around the new year of 1355 he married Fatiu, daughter of the old ruler of Ghana, fulfilling the Ghana betrothal of 1345, and went south across the desert to live there. His first wife was Shamʿa, of a ruling house of the central Sahara (married 1 March 1354). The chronicle reads his going, like Ismāʿīl's in 1359, as the harem clearing the court of the amir's grown brothers.

name: Yūsuf I
note: Died on 1 August 1363 at Ayamonte, on the march into Portugal in the War of Independence, aged 45, after a reign of thirty years. Father of Saʿd, Ismāʿīl, Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī, Muḥammad, Jadīla, Maryam, Fāṭima, ʿĀʾisha and Umm al-Fatḥ.

name: Fāṭima bint Ismāʿīl
note: Married into the ruling house of the Ṭāʾifa of Balansiyya (royal marriage of 22 November 1340).

name: Maryam bint Ismāʿīl
note: Married into the Karasids of Anatolia (royal marriage of 2 August 1353). Married three times. Back at the court of Gharnāṭa, she took a seat in the dīwān on 10 April 1366, in place of Khālid ibn Yaḥyā, and was set to integrating the new lands (save of 6 November 1366).

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl
note: Betrothed on 16 March 1354 to a daughter of the Aydınids of Anatolia. He married her about March 1359 and went to live at the Aydınid court, leaving his seat in the dīwān; the chronicle reads it, like Faraj's going, as the harem clearing the court of the amir's grown brothers.

name: Sayyida of Fezzan
note: Daughter of the ruler of Fezzan, of the house of Murzuq. Betrothed to Yūsuf on 16 November 1337, aged nine. Her father's name is the game's (name_salmama); its proper form is unconfirmed. Married to Yūsuf I while the Jamāʿa of 1344 sat (Trent's account), a marriage that helped inspire the royal harem law of that October.

name: Gideon ben Joshua
note: A Sephardi Jew of Gharnāṭa, of the burghers' estate; at court by 16 November 1337. Died on 14 May 1339: he fell down the stairs.

name: Yaḥyā Raḥḥū
note: A Zenata Berber, founder and head of the house of Raḥḥū; general from 1 September 1339 at the head of the Volunteers of the Faith. The game calls him 'a competent yet fickle figure'. He led the Volunteers of the Faith again from 18 October 1346, when they rose against the united crowns (in the game files his second command is a separate character with the same name, house and birth date; the chronicle keeps them one man). Took Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl's seat in the dīwān in 1355, after Faraj went to Ghana. Died of illness on 18 February 1355, aged 54 by the game's reckoning, soon after taking the seat; the court called it coincidence.

name: Joan d'Oriola
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Balansiyya
note: Ruler of Valencia from its release as a ṭāʾifa on 23 August 1340: a Catalan, Sunni, of the house the game calls Orihuela. The chronicle keeps the Christian name he was born with, as the game does (Trent's decision), so he stays recognisable later.

name: Juan Manuel Enríquez
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya
note: Ruler of Murcia from its release as a ṭāʾifa on 23 August 1340: a Castilian, Sunni. The chronicle keeps the Christian name he was born with, as the game does (Trent's decision), so he stays recognisable later. His host of 410 was destroyed by a Moroccan landing at Málaga on 16 September 1369.

name: Khālid ibn Yaḥyā
note: Son of Yaḥyā Raḥḥū and Qamar, the mother of Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl: born into the Raḥḥū house on 30 December 1342. Took his seat in the dīwān on 2 April 1359, at sixteen, after Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl left for the Aydınid court; set to promoting Andalusī culture. One of the ablest men at court (80/85/78), an architect. Left the dīwān on 10 April 1366, when Maryam bint Ismāʿīl took his seat. A general in the Second Marīnid War: he was thrown back before Cádiz on 26 June 1369, held the line at Antequera on 15 October and won at Almuñécar on 8 November (save of 18 November 1369).

name: Alfonso XI of Castile
note: King of Castile, Granada's overlord; husband of Maria, queen of Portugal.

name: Maria of Portugal
note: Queen of Portugal in her own right and consort of Alfonso XI of Castile; their son Peter is heir to both crowns.

name: Peter of Castile
note: Son of Alfonso XI and Queen Maria, heir to both Castile and Portugal (the 20 May 1343 save).

name: Peter, the Portuguese pretender
note: Queen Maria's younger brother; leads the revolt against her that began on 25 October 1340.

name: Najīb
note: A man of the ʿulamāʾ who appears at court by January 1345, with gifts to rival any in the realm (85/96/76). The game calls him Abuna Najīb al-ʿĀbidīn. On 6 October 1351 he was handed over to Castile at its demand, was baptised, and became Ramiro, a Castilian, taking the learning of Qurṭuba's libraries with him: the second great mind of the court to go over to Castile, after Ibn al-Khaṭīb.

name: Saʿd ibn Yūsuf
note: First son of Yūsuf I and Sayyida of Fezzan, born 18 January 1348 in the second year of the war with the three crowns. Betrothed on 19 January 1351 to Aiman, daughter of the Mamluk Sultan. The same winter the Chancellor reported him a Prodigy: a child predestined, the court said, to leave his name in the history books. His father brought the finest tutors of the Islamic world to Gharnāṭa for him, several Christians among them. Succeeded his father on 1 August 1363 at fifteen, under the regency of Naṣr al-Istijjī until he came of age on 18 January 1364. At his accession his abilities stood at 100/69/100, the prodigy fulfilled. His accession was not clean. Naṣr died on the very day the regency ended, of 'sickness' as the court gave out (a hunting accident, the game says), and Saʿd then married Naṣr's widow Duʿāʾ, his father's Marīnid widow and minister. He began his personal rule with two wives, Aiman the Mamlūk and Duʿāʾ the Marīnid. He knocked Portugal out of the War of Independence on 11 September 1364 and took its south, and by 1365 the court called him Conqueror. His first child, Umm al-Fatḥ, was born to Aiman on 13 December 1364. His son and heir Ismāʿīl was born to Duʿāʾ on 8 March 1366. He won the War of Independence on 5 April 1366.

name: Aiman
note: Daughter of the Mamluk Sultan, betrothed to Saʿd ibn Yūsuf, heir of Granada, on 19 January 1351. Married to Saʿd before he came of age; at his majority in January 1364 she was his only wife, until he also married Duʿāʾ. Mother of Saʿd's first child, Umm al-Fatḥ (born 13 December 1364). Mother of Jadīla bint Saʿd (born 13 December 1368).

name: Duʿāʾ
note: A princess of the Marīnid house of Fās, betrothed to Granada on 18 January 1348 and married to Yūsuf I about 12 August 1354: the one Marīnid bond that outlived Morocco's annulment of its treaties with Granada in 1351. The most capable of the amir's wives, she took Yaḥyā Raḥḥū's seat in the dīwān about 10 March 1355, after his death, under the Powerful Harem law that let women sit in the cabinet. By August 1358 she was widely praised for bringing fresh ideas and practices to the court (the game's 'Foreign Wisdom'), to the nobility's displeasure. Mother of Yūsuf's son Muḥammad (1356–1358). Widowed on 1 August 1363, she married the regent Naṣr al-Istijjī within days. Widowed again a few days after 18 January 1364, when Naṣr died of 'sickness', she then married the young Sultan Saʿd, her late husband Yūsuf's son. That made her his second wife, beside Aiman the Mamlūk. Mother of Saʿd's son and heir Ismāʿīl (born 8 March 1366).

name: Tizemt
note: A princess of the Ḥafṣid house of Tūnis, betrothed to Granada on 23 July 1345 and married to Yūsuf I on 19 November 1354, three months after his Marīnid marriage. Her name is Berber (Amazigh).

name: Fatiu
note: Daughter of the old ruler of Ghana. The Ghana betrothal of 8 September 1345 was fulfilled by her marriage to Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl, the amir's elder brother, who went south to live in Ghana with her (around the new year of 1355). Mother of Zineb, Faraj's daughter born in Ghana.

name: Shamʿa
note: Of a ruling house of the central Sahara (the game's AAA43). First wife of Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl, by the royal marriage of 1 March 1354, before his second marriage to Fatiu of Ghana. When Faraj went south to Ghana she stayed in Granada with his child.

name: ʿĀʾisha bint Faraj
note: Daughter of Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl and Shamʿa, born 28 March 1355 in Granada, about three months after her father had gone south to Ghana.

name: Zineb bint Faraj
note: Daughter of Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl and Fatiu, born in Ghana after her father went south (Fatiu was pregnant in the save of 16 June 1355; the birth date isn't recorded yet).

name: Naṣr al-Istijjī
note: A noble of the house of Istijja (Écija). The game made him regent during Yūsuf I's Hajj (the chronicle gave that regency to Faraj); on Yūsuf's death in August 1363 he became regent for the young Saʿd, and at once married Duʿāʾ, the late amir's Marīnid widow and minister. The game calls him a babbling buffoon. His regency ended when Saʿd came of age on 18 January 1364, and he died that same day. The court called it 'sickness'; the game records a hunting accident. Duʿāʾ, his widow, married the young sultan soon after.

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf
note: Heir to his half-brother Saʿd until Saʿd's son Ismāʿīl was born on 8 March 1366 (saves of 11 September 1364 and 6 November 1366).

name: Murād
note: Granadan general in the War of Independence. He chased the joined armies of Portugal and Aragon halfway across Iberia and broke them at Zafra on 3 August 1364. Then, on 10 and 11 September, he destroyed their remnants one after the other before Lisbon (save of 11 September 1364). He threw back the Aragonese at Cañete (14 July 1365). At San Clemente (6 January 1366) he destroyed the last Castilian army in the field, commanded by the renegade Ibn al-Khaṭīb (save of 5 April 1366). In the Second Marīnid War he destroyed the sultan of Fās's own force at Cádiz (11 November 1368), threw the first Marīnid landing back into the sea at Marbella (8 February 1369) and retook Jerez (28 April).

name: Umm al-Fatḥ bint Saʿd
note: First child of Sultan Saʿd, born to Aiman the Mamlūk three months after the Portuguese peace. She shares her name, 'mother of victory', with her aunt, Yūsuf I's youngest daughter.

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd
note: Son and heir of Sultan Saʿd, born to Duʿāʾ the Marīnid on 8 March 1366, a month before the Peace of Independence.

name: Rodrigo of Silves
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb
note: A Portuguese lord, now a Muslim, set over the Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb when Granada released the Portuguese south as its vassal on 13 April 1366 (save of 6 November 1366). In September 1368 Castile guaranteed his ṭāʾifa's independence, and Granada backed the loyalists against it.

name: Abū ʿInān Fāris
note: Marīnid sultan of Fās. He declared the Second War for the Submission of Granada on 24 October 1368 and led the first Marīnid force across the Strait himself. Murād destroyed it at Cádiz on 11 November 1368 (save of 18 November 1369).

name: ʿUthmān
note: The Marīnid general of the 1369 counterattack. He relieved Cádiz and threw Khālid back before it (2 and 26 June 1369). Then he marched on the heart of the realm and was stopped at Antequera (15 October 1369).
